Company profile: US imaging company; once a dominant film and camera brand, later restructured around commercial printing and imaging.
Documented business problem: Kodak did not convert its early digital-imaging knowledge into a durable mass-market digital-camera and services position as film demand structurally declined.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The strategic issue was not simply failing to invent digital photography. It was the difficulty of replacing a profitable film-and-processing ecosystem with a lower-margin digital model and new capabilities.
Business impact / signal: Kodak filed for Chapter 11 protection in January 2012 and pursued asset sales and a narrower operating focus.
Documented company / regulator response: The Chapter 11 plan focused on liquidity, monetising non-core intellectual property and concentrating on commercial imaging and printing.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Create explicit cannibalisation milestones; shift capital and talent toward the emerging customer workflow before the legacy profit pool collapses.
LinkedIn post angle: Kodak had the technology. Why was the business model harder to reinvent than the product?
Evidence type: Primary – SEC filing / company restructuring record

Company profile: US video-rental chain with stores, physical inventory and a large customer base before streaming became mainstream.
Documented business problem: The company failed to transition its store-led rental economics quickly enough as customers moved toward mail subscriptions and digital streaming.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Stores, late fees, inventory and geographic footprint were embedded in the economics. A digital transition required cannibalising the legacy network and investing in a different technology and content-access model.
Business impact / signal: Blockbuster entered Chapter 11 in September 2010.
Documented company / regulator response: The company sought court-supervised restructuring; the filing documents the bankruptcy process rather than a successful turnaround.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Build a migration plan that measures customer retention and contribution margin in the new channel, not just the number of stores preserved.
LinkedIn post angle: A strong incumbent can lose when it protects the channel instead of following the customer.

Company profile: Finnish mobile-phone maker that led the handset market before iOS and Android reshaped the smartphone ecosystem.
Documented business problem: Nokia struggled to respond to the smartphone shift and to build a competitive software and app ecosystem at the pace of new rivals.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The challenge combined platform fragmentation, organisational decision-making, developer ecosystem weakness and a slower response to the new basis of competition.
Business impact / signal: Nokia sold its Devices & Services business to Microsoft in 2014 after announcing the transaction in 2013.
Documented company / regulator response: The case literature analyses the strategic and organisational causes; the company exited handset manufacturing through the Microsoft transaction.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Compete on the whole customer ecosystem—operating system, developers, services and updates—not hardware specifications alone.
LinkedIn post angle: Nokia did not just lose a phone battle. It lost the platform battle.

Company profile: Canadian smartphone and enterprise-security company known for physical keyboards and secure email.
Documented business problem: BlackBerry's product portfolio and launch cadence lost relevance as customers shifted to touch-first smartphones and app-rich platforms.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The problem was ecosystem breadth and consumer experience, not only device design: developers, apps, browser experience and timing increasingly shaped purchase decisions.
Business impact / signal: The company launched BlackBerry 10 and restructured its business; SEC reporting described weak device shipments and competitive pressure.
Documented company / regulator response: BlackBerry's filing describes declining shipments and a portfolio that struggled to meet consumer demand for high-end devices and LTE.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Prioritise a small number of customer segments where security is a differentiator; partner for ecosystem gaps rather than trying to rebuild everything.
LinkedIn post angle: When the product is technically good but the ecosystem is missing, what exactly is the customer buying?

Company profile: US internet portal and digital-advertising business that held large user accounts and personal data.
Documented business problem: Major data breaches became a material transaction and trust issue during the Verizon acquisition process.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Security is not only an IT control. In a data-heavy platform, weak detection, disclosure and governance can become a commercial liability affecting valuation and user trust.
Business impact / signal: The announced acquisition price was reduced from about $4.83bn to $4.48bn after breach disclosures; the SEC later examined disclosure practices.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC filing records the purchase-price adjustment and the breach-related transaction context.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Treat security as board-level enterprise risk: inventory critical data, test incident response, disclose promptly and make cyber controls part of diligence.
LinkedIn post angle: A cyber incident can become a valuation problem, not just a technology problem.

Company profile: Canadian retail expansion by US retailer Target, involving hundreds of new stores and a new merchandising and supply-chain system.
Documented business problem: Product and inventory master data were unreliable during the Canadian rollout, contributing to empty shelves and excess stock in the wrong locations.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Bad item data propagates across ordering, replenishment, distribution and store execution. The issue was a foundational data-governance and systems-integration failure, not merely poor store merchandising.
Business impact / signal: Target exited Canada and sought creditor protection for the Canadian business in 2015.
Documented company / regulator response: The Eighth Circuit record discusses item-data accuracy and operational failures in the Canadian rollout.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Run a controlled launch with verified product master data, end-to-end testing, store-level exception dashboards and explicit go/no-go gates.
LinkedIn post angle: A retailer can have inventory in the network and still have nothing useful on the shelf.

Company profile: US department-store retailer that changed its pricing architecture under CEO Ron Johnson.
Documented business problem: The retailer replaced coupons and frequent promotions with an everyday-low-price approach that customers did not adopt as expected.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Management redesigned the price architecture around an internal logic without adequately preserving customer habits, price cues and the emotional reward of promotions.
Business impact / signal: Comparable sales fell sharply after the strategy change; the company later reintroduced promotional pricing.
Documented company / regulator response: SEC results showed a 21.7% comparable-sales decline in the cited quarter; contemporary analysis documented the customer response.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Pilot pricing changes by customer segment and store cluster; measure conversion, basket size, margin and repeat visits before a national reset.
LinkedIn post angle: A pricing strategy can be mathematically neat and still fail the way customers actually shop.

Company profile: US department-store and home-services retailer operating Sears and Kmart brands.
Documented business problem: The retailer struggled with declining store relevance, asset-heavy operations, weak sales and a difficult financial position.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The business faced a reinforcing loop: weaker traffic reduced store productivity; underinvestment degraded the customer proposition; fixed costs and debt limited reinvestment.
Business impact / signal: Sears Holdings filed for Chapter 11 in October 2018.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC filing confirms the Chapter 11 petition; this is a documented insolvency outcome, while the causal diagnosis is analytical.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Simplify the footprint early, ring-fence viable categories, improve in-stock rates and reinvest only where store-level contribution economics work.
LinkedIn post angle: A legacy brand cannot cut its way back to relevance if the customer proposition keeps deteriorating.

Company profile: US mobile-first short-form premium video subscription service founded by Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman.
Documented business problem: Quibi struggled to convert a large funding base and star-led content slate into sustained paid viewing and shut down within months of launch.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The proposition asked users to pay for short premium episodes in a market where free short-form platforms and long-form streaming already had strong habits and distribution.
Business impact / signal: The company announced a wind-down roughly six months after launch.
Documented company / regulator response: Contemporary reporting documented the closure and the company's inability to attract sufficient paying subscribers.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Validate usage occasions and willingness to pay before committing to a large content budget; test retention cohorts, not launch awareness.
LinkedIn post angle: A product can be well-funded and beautifully produced but still fail to earn a place in someone's daily routine.

Company profile: Google cloud-gaming service that streamed games without a dedicated console.
Documented business problem: Stadia did not gain the user traction expected to sustain the service and its commercial model.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Cloud delivery solved one part of the problem, but gaming platforms also need compelling content, developer commitment, user acquisition and a durable catalogue.
Business impact / signal: Google announced the shutdown, offered refunds for eligible purchases and closed Stadia in January 2023.
Documented company / regulator response: Google's official blog explained that the service had not gained the traction expected.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Secure anchor content and developer economics before scaling infrastructure; prove repeat engagement and lifetime value before expanding the platform.
LinkedIn post angle: Infrastructure is not the product. In gaming, the content ecosystem is the product.

Company profile: Hewlett-Packard acquired UK enterprise-software company Autonomy in 2011.
Documented business problem: HP recorded a large impairment after acquiring Autonomy; HP said the majority related to accounting improprieties and disclosure failures at Autonomy before acquisition.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The case highlights the danger of relying on reported growth and headline valuation without enough forensic diligence on revenue quality, customer contracts and accounting judgements.
Business impact / signal: HP recorded an $8.8bn impairment charge and pursued legal action.
Documented company / regulator response: HP's SEC filing describes the impairment and its stated reasons; allegations and litigation should be described with attribution.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use independent revenue-quality testing, customer confirmations, cash-conversion analysis and integration risk gates before closing an acquisition.
LinkedIn post angle: The real due-diligence question is not 'How fast is revenue growing?' but 'How real and repeatable is the revenue?'

Company profile: Quaker Oats acquired beverage brand Snapple in 1994 and later sold it after a short, costly ownership period.
Documented business problem: Quaker struggled to manage Snapple's distinctive distribution, brand and entrepreneurial operating model after acquisition.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The buyer's capabilities in a different beverage system did not automatically transfer. Integration can destroy the local relationships and speed that made an acquired brand valuable.
Business impact / signal: Quaker sold Snapple at a substantial loss after about 27 months.
Documented company / regulator response: Stanford's case and contemporary reporting document the acquisition and resale.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Map the acquired company's sources of advantage before integration; preserve critical distributors, decision rights and brand voice while measuring synergy separately.
LinkedIn post angle: An acquisition can destroy value when the buyer integrates away the reason the target was successful.

Company profile: US daily-deal marketplace connecting consumers with discounted local merchant offers.
Documented business problem: Groupon's deal-led model created a risk that merchants received low-quality, promotion-sensitive customers rather than profitable repeat business.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The platform optimised for deal volume and consumer discounts; merchant retention depends on incremental contribution after discount, redemption capacity and repeat purchase.
Business impact / signal: The SEC filing details a revenue model reliant on merchant promotions and the company's operating risks.
Documented company / regulator response: The filing is used as evidence of the model and risks, not proof that every merchant lost money.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Measure merchant-level incrementality, repeat rate and contribution margin; stop selling promotions that simply subsidise customers who would have visited anyway.
LinkedIn post angle: A marketplace must create value for both sides—not just generate a high volume of transactions.

Company profile: Connected-fitness company selling exercise equipment, subscriptions and digital workouts.
Documented business problem: Demand surged during lockdowns, but the company was left with excess capacity and a cost base built for demand that did not persist.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The failure was a forecasting and capacity-planning mismatch: a temporary demand shock was treated too much like a permanent demand curve.
Business impact / signal: Peloton announced restructuring, workforce reductions and changes to manufacturing and distribution arrangements.
Documented company / regulator response: Its SEC filing documents restructuring and capacity changes following demand normalisation.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Separate temporary demand from structural growth; use flexible production, scenario-based inventory commitments and demand-triggered capacity expansion.
LinkedIn post angle: The danger is not growing too fast. It is building permanent costs around temporary demand.

Company profile: US semiconductor designer and manufacturer with an integrated-device manufacturing model.
Documented business problem: Process-node delays weakened Intel's product cadence and gave fabless rivals using foundries an opportunity to compete on leading-edge manufacturing.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Manufacturing leadership is a strategic asset only while process execution, yields and product design stay aligned. Delays compound because product roadmaps depend on manufacturing milestones.
Business impact / signal: Intel disclosed process delays and, in 2024, recorded a significant Gaudi-related inventory charge.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC annual report describes manufacturing challenges, competitive pressures and inventory charges.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use milestone-based capacity investment, independent yield gates and contingency foundry capacity; disclose roadmap risk before it becomes a customer surprise.
LinkedIn post angle: In semiconductors, a delayed process node can become a multi-year competitive problem.

Company profile: Meta's virtual-reality and augmented-reality division developing Quest devices, software and future computing platforms.
Documented business problem: Reality Labs generated substantial revenue but continued to report very large operating losses as Meta invested in long-term immersive technology.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): This is a capital-allocation challenge, not proof that the strategy is inherently wrong: the board must balance long-horizon option value with cash burn, adoption and monetisation milestones.
Business impact / signal: Meta's 2025 filing reported Reality Labs revenue of about $2.2bn and an operating loss of about $19.2bn.
Documented company / regulator response: The 10-K quantifies segment revenue and operating loss; it does not establish a final verdict on long-term value.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Define staged investment gates tied to active usage, retention, developer ecosystem, gross margin and a credible path to unit economics.
LinkedIn post angle: How do you fund a 10-year technology bet without allowing it to become an unlimited cheque?

Company profile: US electric-vehicle maker that attempted to scale Model 3 production rapidly in 2017–2018.
Documented business problem: The Model 3 ramp encountered bottlenecks in manufacturing automation and the wider production system.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The issue showed that factory throughput is constrained by the whole line, including parts, people, quality checks and process balancing—not simply the degree of automation.
Business impact / signal: Tesla simplified parts of the production process and reintroduced more manual work in some areas while working through the ramp.
Documented company / regulator response: Tesla's SEC filings and contemporaneous interviews describe production challenges and adjustments.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Design production around stable takt time and quality; automate only repeatable processes and keep a rapid manual fallback for bottleneck stations.
LinkedIn post angle: Automation does not fix a broken process. It can make the bottleneck more expensive.

Company profile: US consumer-products company historically reliant on direct selling and a well-known food-storage brand.
Documented business problem: The company entered Chapter 11 after years of financial pressure and difficulty adapting its operating and distribution model.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Brand awareness does not guarantee channel relevance. Direct-selling economics and an ageing route to market can weaken against modern retail, e-commerce and changing consumer behaviour.
Business impact / signal: Tupperware filed for Chapter 11 in September 2024.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC filing confirms the bankruptcy petition; the channel diagnosis is an analytical interpretation.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Rebuild distribution around where customers shop, simplify the portfolio and separate brand revitalisation from the restructuring of liabilities.
LinkedIn post angle: A famous brand can outlive the business model that made it famous.

Company profile: US home-goods retailer with a large physical store base and a merchandising model under pressure.
Documented business problem: The company filed for Chapter 11 after prolonged sales and liquidity pressure.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A retailer needs working capital, differentiated assortment and supplier confidence. When those deteriorate together, empty shelves and lower traffic can reinforce the cash crisis.
Business impact / signal: The company filed for Chapter 11 in April 2023.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC filing confirms the bankruptcy filing; the operating diagnosis is analytical and should be presented as such.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Prioritise high-velocity categories, protect supplier terms, close structurally unprofitable stores early and use weekly cash-and-inventory controls.
LinkedIn post angle: Retail failure often appears as a sales problem before it becomes a working-capital crisis.

Company profile: Chinese property developer with extensive development projects and a large debt-funded balance sheet.
Documented business problem: A debt-heavy property model came under pressure as sales and refinancing conditions weakened, leaving the group unable to meet obligations.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The balance sheet relied on continued access to capital and pre-sales. When buyer confidence and funding weakened, long project cycles made liabilities difficult to refinance.
Business impact / signal: A Hong court ordered the company wound up in January 2024; liquidators were appointed.
Documented company / regulator response: The liquidator's official site documents the winding-up and liquidation process.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Match debt maturities to project cash flows, ring-fence customer funds and disclose project-level liquidity and completion risks.
LinkedIn post angle: Growth funded by leverage works until the refinancing window closes.

Company profile: US aerospace manufacturer; the 737 MAX was a high-volume narrow-body aircraft family.
Documented business problem: The 737 MAX crashes and subsequent grounding exposed design, certification, training and safety-governance failures.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The core management lesson is that safety-critical design decisions cannot be subordinated to schedule, cost or competitive positioning; risk information must travel upward without filtering.
Business impact / signal: The aircraft was grounded worldwide; Boeing made design changes, training changes and faced regulatory and legal consequences.
Documented company / regulator response: The US House committee report details technical, organisational and oversight failures.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Create independent safety authority, transparent hazard escalation, human-factors testing and board-level monitoring of unresolved safety findings.
LinkedIn post angle: When speed to market conflicts with safety, the cost of the wrong trade-off is measured in lives and trust.

Company profile: Major aerospace structures supplier producing fuselage sections and other components for aircraft manufacturers.
Documented business problem: The FAA's 737-9 MAX review identified manufacturing-process-control and parts-handling issues in the Boeing production system and audited supplier processes, including Spirit AeroSystems.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A complex supply chain needs shared quality ownership. When the OEM and supplier operate with weak process discipline or unclear handoffs, inspection cannot reliably compensate.
Business impact / signal: The FAA increased scrutiny and Boeing was required to prepare a 90-day safety and quality action plan.
Documented company / regulator response: The FAA update documents audit findings and the production-control response; it does not attribute every finding solely to one supplier.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use common process-control plans, traceability, supplier capability audits and stop-work authority that is independent of output targets.
LinkedIn post angle: You cannot inspect quality into a process that was not controlled at the source.

Company profile: US aerospace and defence group whose Pratt & Whitney division makes geared turbofan engines used on commercial aircraft.
Documented business problem: A powder-metal manufacturing issue in some GTF engines required accelerated inspections and removals from service.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A specialised component problem became a fleet-wide planning challenge because engines, spare capacity, maintenance slots and airline schedules are tightly coupled.
Business impact / signal: RTX disclosed expected engine removals and a multi-year financial impact while coordinating inspections and repairs.
Documented company / regulator response: RTX filings and company disclosures describe the powder-metal issue and its expected costs.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Build a fleet-level risk model linking component traceability, inspection intervals, spare-engine capacity and customer recovery plans.
LinkedIn post angle: A small component defect can create a network-wide capacity problem.

Company profile: Quick-service restaurant chain whose UK operations relied on a network of franchisees and third-party logistics.
Documented business problem: A distributor transition caused chicken-supply disruption, forcing many UK restaurants to close or operate with limited menus.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The transition was treated as a supplier switch, but it was a critical service-continuity event. A single-point logistics dependency left little resilience when the new network failed.
Business impact / signal: KFC communicated store closures and gradually reopened restaurants as supply recovered.
Documented company / regulator response: Company disclosures and annual-report material describe the distributor transition and business impact.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use phased cutover, dual-run logistics, regional safety stock, route simulation and clear service-level triggers before changing a critical supplier.
LinkedIn post angle: A supplier transition is not complete when the contract is signed. It is complete when the customer still gets the product.

Company profile: Global coffeehouse chain with a large company-operated store network.
Documented business problem: Rapid expansion and inconsistent store experience weakened the customer proposition and prompted a major US store rationalisation.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Store count had become a growth proxy. The more important system was service quality, coffee standards, employee capability and store economics.
Business impact / signal: Starbucks closed about 600 underperforming US stores and refocused on product and store experience.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC annual report documents closures and restructuring actions.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Set a service-experience scorecard alongside store growth; use customer wait times, product consistency, labour coverage and store contribution to guide expansion.
LinkedIn post angle: The fastest way to damage a service brand is to scale locations faster than the experience.

Company profile: US pizza chain operating through company-owned and franchised stores.
Documented business problem: Customer feedback and public criticism exposed a product-quality perception problem for the brand.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Marketing cannot permanently hide a product problem. The company needed to improve the actual eating experience and be willing to acknowledge the gap openly.
Business impact / signal: Domino's launched a product-focused turnaround campaign and reformulated its core pizza.
Documented company / regulator response: The case archive documents the 'Pizza Turnaround' campaign and product response.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Tie customer feedback to product reformulation and franchise execution; measure repeat purchase and complaint trends rather than campaign reach alone.
LinkedIn post angle: The most credible marketing campaign may begin with admitting the product is not good enough.

Company profile: German automotive group with a global passenger-car and commercial-vehicle portfolio.
Documented business problem: Volkswagen used software defeat devices to circumvent emissions testing in diesel vehicles.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): This was not a technical glitch; it reflected governance and culture failures where regulatory compliance and truthful disclosure lost to performance and market-positioning targets.
Business impact / signal: The company faced recalls, litigation, leadership changes and substantial remediation costs.
Documented company / regulator response: The EPA documents violations; INSEAD's case study examines organisational culture and decision-making.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Create independent compliance testing, protect dissenting engineering voices and link executive incentives to verified safety and environmental outcomes.
LinkedIn post angle: When internal metrics reward the result more than the truth, misconduct becomes an operating risk.
Evidence type: Primary – EPA regulator record + academic case

Company profile: US automaker with a large passenger-vehicle portfolio.
Documented business problem: An ignition-switch defect led to recalls and investigations after warnings were not escalated and acted on quickly enough.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The underlying issue was not only component design. It was the failure of safety information, responsibility and decision rights to move through the organisation in time.
Business impact / signal: GM recalled millions of vehicles and implemented a compensation and safety-response process.
Documented company / regulator response: The US DOT Inspector General reviewed NHTSA's handling of vehicle defects; the report documents recall scale and safety failures.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Create one defect owner, a no-blame escalation channel, time-bound investigation SLAs and direct board reporting for safety-critical signals.
LinkedIn post angle: A warning that sits in a spreadsheet is not a control. It becomes a control only when someone is accountable for action.
Evidence type: Primary – US DOT Inspector General report

Company profile: South Korean electronics maker; the Note7 was a flagship premium smartphone.
Documented business problem: Battery defects caused some Note7 devices to overheat and catch fire, leading to recalls and discontinuation.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The launch and replacement process showed the risk of treating a safety defect as a component issue before fully understanding the failure mechanism.
Business impact / signal: Samsung recalled devices, halted sales and ended production of the Note7.
Documented company / regulator response: The US CPSC issued recall notices; Samsung published statements about the product response.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use supplier-level battery traceability, independent stress testing and a stop-ship rule until root cause is verified across replacement units.
LinkedIn post angle: The second failure is often more damaging than the first: it shows the root cause was not understood.

Company profile: Indian packaged-food business selling Maggi instant noodles through a nationwide distribution network.
Documented business problem: Maggi noodles were withdrawn from sale after food-safety concerns and regulatory action related to testing, labelling and product approval.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The crisis showed how a high-penetration brand can face a trust shock when product testing, regulatory confidence and communication are not aligned.
Business impact / signal: The Bombay High Court set aside the nationwide ban; the company conducted fresh testing and relaunched Maggi in November 2015.
Documented company / regulator response: The Government of India release records the regulatory order; Nestlé's timeline records the subsequent tests and relaunch.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Publish independently verified test protocols, maintain batch traceability and prepare a plain-language crisis communication plan with regulators and consumers.
LinkedIn post angle: Brand equity is earned over years but can be tested in a single product-safety crisis.

Company profile: UK retail bank that migrated millions of customer accounts to a new IT platform in 2018.
Documented business problem: A major IT migration caused customers to lose access to online and mobile banking and disrupted branch and payment services.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The bank's migration control and contingency planning were inadequate for the scale and customer criticality of the change.
Business impact / signal: The FCA fined TSB for operational-resilience failings; service recovery took months.
Documented company / regulator response: The FCA release describes the migration failure and enforcement action.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use parallel-run testing, customer-impact simulations, staged migration cohorts and a tested rollback path before switching core banking infrastructure.
LinkedIn post angle: A technology transformation is successful only when the customer experiences a better service—not when the system goes live.

Company profile: US market-making and trading firm using automated electronic trading systems.
Documented business problem: A defective software deployment triggered erroneous orders and a loss of roughly $460m in less than an hour.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The firm lacked adequate release controls, deployment consistency and clear ownership of kill switches and system alerts.
Business impact / signal: The SEC charged Knight Capital; the company later accepted a settlement and strengthened controls.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC release details the defective deployment, missed alerts and trading losses.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Enforce one-click rollback, release certification across every server, canary deployment and a rehearsed kill switch with named authority.
LinkedIn post angle: A software release process is part of financial risk management when code can move real money.

Company profile: US retail bank with a nationwide branch network and aggressive cross-selling targets.
Documented business problem: Employees opened unauthorised customer accounts in order to meet sales goals and incentive targets.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The problem was a control-system failure: targets and local pressure rewarded account volume without enough validation of customer consent and conduct.
Business impact / signal: Regulators imposed major penalties; the bank changed sales practices and oversight arrangements.
Documented company / regulator response: The CFPB documented millions of potentially unauthorised accounts and a $100m penalty.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Replace raw product-count targets with verified customer outcomes; monitor consent, complaint patterns, reversals and employee pressure signals.
LinkedIn post angle: If the incentive is wrong, even a talented team can produce the wrong behaviour at scale.

Company profile: US credit-reporting agency holding sensitive financial and identity data for consumers.
Documented business problem: A cyberattack exposed personal information affecting about 147 million people.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The business risk was amplified by the sensitivity and scale of the data, patching and vulnerability-management controls, and governance around incident response.
Business impact / signal: Equifax agreed to a settlement of up to $700m with US authorities and consumers.
Documented company / regulator response: The CFPB enforcement page describes the breach and settlement.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Maintain an asset inventory, automated patch SLAs, independent penetration testing and board-level reporting on unresolved critical vulnerabilities.
LinkedIn post angle: When data is the product, cybersecurity is part of the product's quality promise.

Company profile: Global hotel group that acquired Starwood, inheriting a large reservation and loyalty-data platform.
Documented business problem: Multiple data breaches affected hundreds of millions of guest records; the FTC required stronger data-security practices.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): M&A diligence must include cyber controls, data lineage and retention practices. Acquiring the business also means acquiring the inherited data risk.
Business impact / signal: The FTC finalised an order requiring a robust data-security programme and additional customer protections.
Documented company / regulator response: The FTC release documents the breaches and requirements in its order.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Make cyber diligence a deal-closing condition; minimise retained data, unify identity controls and test breach response across acquired systems.
LinkedIn post angle: An acquisition integrates customer data on day one—even if the security culture is still separate.

Company profile: UK automotive manufacturer with plants, suppliers and dealerships across multiple markets.
Documented business problem: A cyber incident forced the company to shut down systems, severely disrupting retail and production operations.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): In a digitally connected factory, IT downtime can quickly become a physical supply-chain and revenue problem.
Business impact / signal: JLR said it took systems offline and worked with cybersecurity specialists and authorities; it reported no evidence at that point that customer data had been stolen.
Documented company / regulator response: The company's incident statement describes the operational disruption and initial response.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Build tested offline production modes, segmented operational technology, supplier continuity protocols and recovery-time objectives by plant.
LinkedIn post angle: Cybersecurity is now an operations discipline: when systems stop, factories and dealers can stop too.

Company profile: US autonomous-vehicle company operating robotaxi services in selected cities.
Documented business problem: Cruise faced regulatory action after its reporting of a serious pedestrian crash was found incomplete.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Autonomous systems need safety performance and transparent incident disclosure. Trust depends on truthful reporting as much as technical capability.
Business impact / signal: NHTSA issued a consent order and required a civil penalty related to crash-reporting failures.
Documented company / regulator response: NHTSA's consent-order release documents the reporting issue.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Create a single incident command centre, regulator notification deadlines and independent safety review before resuming public-road operations.
LinkedIn post angle: In a high-trust technology business, how you report a failure is part of the product.

Company profile: Indian electric two-wheeler manufacturer with a direct-to-consumer sales and service network.
Documented business problem: The CCPA ordered a detailed investigation after receiving more than 10,000 consumer complaints about product and service deficiencies.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A fast-growing installed base creates a service obligation. If service capacity, spare parts and grievance resolution lag deliveries, brand trust deteriorates.
Business impact / signal: The CCPA directed an investigation; the complaints were not all adjudicated findings against the company.
Documented company / regulator response: Reporting documented the 10,644 complaints and the regulator's notice.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Track first-time-fix rate, parts fill rate, repeat repair, complaint ageing and service capacity per 1,000 vehicles; link expansion to service readiness.
LinkedIn post angle: For a vehicle brand, the real customer journey begins after delivery—not when the booking is paid.

Company profile: Global quick-service restaurant operator with a mix of company-operated and franchised restaurants.
Documented business problem: The company's SEC disclosure identifies staffing availability and execution as risks to speed of service and customer satisfaction.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): In labour-intensive service systems, staffing is an operational input to throughput and experience—not simply an HR cost line.
Business impact / signal: The filing describes workforce and staffing challenges as operating risks; it does not claim a company-wide service failure.
Documented company / regulator response: McDonald's annual filing identifies staffing and service execution risks.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Forecast labour by daypart and demand; monitor wait time, order accuracy, employee turnover and store-level schedule adherence together.
LinkedIn post angle: A store can be fully stocked and still fail the customer if it is not staffed for the demand curve.
Evidence type: Primary – SEC annual filing / disclosed risk

Company profile: US fast-casual restaurant chain using fresh ingredients and store-level food preparation.
Documented business problem: Foodborne-illness incidents were linked to failures in store-level adherence to food-safety protocols, including illness reporting and temperature controls.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A policy is not a control if staffing, training and local management incentives make it hard to follow. Execution gaps at individual stores can scale into a national brand crisis.
Business impact / signal: Chipotle agreed to a $25m fine and an enhanced food-safety compliance programme; it added controls and monitoring.
Documented company / regulator response: The Department of Justice described incidents and the required compliance programme; Chipotle's current safety page explains enhanced procedures.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use real-time HACCP monitoring, mandatory illness exclusion, shift-level food-safety ownership and unannounced audit sampling.
LinkedIn post angle: Food safety is won or lost in the last 10 metres: the store, the shift and the person handling the food.
Evidence type: Primary – US DOJ deferred prosecution agreement

Company profile: US commercial bank concentrated in technology companies, venture-backed firms and their investors.
Documented business problem: A highly concentrated, uninsured-deposit base and interest-rate exposure created a rapid liquidity crisis when depositors withdrew funds.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The bank's asset-liability duration and deposit concentration were poorly matched; the risk became systemic when trust and liquidity moved together.
Business impact / signal: SVB failed in March 2023 after rapid deposit outflows; the Federal Reserve OIG reviewed supervisory and bank-management failures.
Documented company / regulator response: The Fed OIG report documents the failure and weaknesses in risk management and supervision.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Stress-test correlated withdrawals, hedge duration exposures, diversify funding and maintain a liquidity playbook for a 24-hour digital run.
LinkedIn post angle: A bank run can happen at app speed when deposits are concentrated and confidence disappears.

Company profile: Swiss global bank with investment banking, wealth management and a long history of major scandals.
Documented business problem: Repeated scandals, risk-management failures and loss of client confidence triggered severe withdrawals and a crisis that led to its takeover by UBS.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A series of isolated-looking incidents can become one confidence problem when the organisation fails to demonstrate that lessons have been learned.
Business impact / signal: FINMA described strategy implementation and governance deficiencies; UBS agreed to acquire Credit Suisse in 2023.
Documented company / regulator response: FINMA's review explains weaknesses in strategy, governance and supervisory intervention.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use a single enterprise-risk remediation office with board-owned milestones; close repeat findings and report client outflows alongside risk metrics.
LinkedIn post angle: The biggest risk is not one scandal. It is the market deciding that the next scandal is inevitable.

Company profile: German payments company whose growth story collapsed after accounting irregularities came to light.
Documented business problem: Wirecard's collapse exposed significant weaknesses in financial oversight, auditing and supervisory coordination.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Fast growth in complex cross-border payments can obscure where cash is held, who controls it and whether third-party balances are independently verifiable.
Business impact / signal: The company entered insolvency; ESMA reviewed deficiencies in German supervision and enforcement.
Documented company / regulator response: ESMA's report documents supervisory deficiencies; use 'alleged' or 'reported' for specific criminal conduct unless citing a final judgment.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Confirm cash directly with banks, independently audit third-party acquiring relationships and separate revenue recognition from partner-provided attestations.
LinkedIn post angle: In fintech, growth numbers are not proof of cash. Independent verification is the control.

Company profile: Cryptocurrency exchange group that collapsed after a liquidity crisis and revelations about relationships with Alameda Research.
Documented business problem: The SEC alleged that customer funds were misused and that Alameda received undisclosed preferential treatment.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The fundamental controls are segregation of customer assets, independent governance, transparent related-party exposure and accurate liquidity reporting.
Business impact / signal: FTX filed for bankruptcy; the SEC brought civil fraud charges against founder Sam Bankman-Fried.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC release states the allegations; distinguish allegations from adjudicated findings when writing.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Segregate client assets, reconcile wallets independently, prohibit undisclosed related-party lending and publish audited reserves and liabilities.
LinkedIn post angle: A financial platform cannot treat customer money as working capital.

Company profile: US health-technology startup that claimed to perform many blood tests from small blood samples.
Documented business problem: The SEC charged Theranos and its founder with defrauding investors through misleading claims about its technology and business performance.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The organisation's claims outpaced independently validated technical performance; secrecy and concentrated founder control weakened challenge and verification.
Business impact / signal: The company shut down; the SEC brought fraud charges and the business ceased operations.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC release records the charges and alleged misrepresentations.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Require clinical validation, independent scientific governance and clear separation between investor communications and verified product capabilities.
LinkedIn post angle: In deep tech, a compelling story is not a substitute for repeatable evidence.

Company profile: US flexible-office provider leasing long-term office space and reselling memberships and shorter-term desks.
Documented business problem: The company faced a mismatch between long-term lease obligations and more flexible, shorter-duration customer revenue, culminating in Chapter 11.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The model carried property-market and occupancy risk while selling flexibility to customers. Growth magnified fixed commitments before unit economics were consistently proven.
Business impact / signal: WeWork filed for Chapter 11 in November 2023 and pursued restructuring.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC filing confirms the bankruptcy petition; the lease-duration diagnosis is an analytical reading of the business model.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Match lease duration to customer commitments, use asset-light management contracts and enforce city-level contribution-margin hurdles.
LinkedIn post angle: Selling flexibility is dangerous when your own cost base is inflexible.

Company profile: UK construction and facilities-management contractor with large public-sector and infrastructure contracts.
Documented business problem: Carillion's debt and cash pressures worsened as revenues and contract performance deteriorated; it entered compulsory liquidation in 2018.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Long contracts can report accounting profit while cash is trapped in delayed payments, cost overruns, claims and underpriced bids.
Business impact / signal: The company entered compulsory liquidation; parliamentary analysis documented rising debt and business fragility.
Documented company / regulator response: The UK Parliament briefing records debt growth and the company's collapse.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Price contracts using downside scenarios, track cash margin by project, stop bidding below risk-adjusted returns and escalate loss-making contracts early.
LinkedIn post angle: Revenue is vanity when a contractor cannot convert its projects into cash.

Company profile: US investment bank with major mortgage and capital-markets exposure.
Documented business problem: Lehman's use of Repo 105 transactions temporarily removed assets from its balance sheet around reporting dates, obscuring leverage.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A liquidity and solvency problem was made harder to see when reporting choices created a misleading picture of the balance sheet.
Business impact / signal: Lehman filed for bankruptcy in September 2008; the examiner's report described accounting and governance issues.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC testimony references the examiner's findings on Repo 105.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Report leverage on an economically transparent basis, monitor off-balance-sheet exposures and align risk reporting with daily liquidity rather than quarter-end optics.
LinkedIn post angle: If a balance sheet looks healthier only at quarter-end, the business may not be healthy at all.
Evidence type: Primary – SEC testimony referencing examiner report

Company profile: US insurance group with a large financial-products business selling credit-default swap protection.
Documented business problem: AIG faced severe liquidity pressure as collateral calls rose on its credit-default swap portfolio during the financial crisis.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The business had written exposures whose mark-to-market and collateral requirements could accelerate faster than the group could raise liquidity.
Business impact / signal: The Federal Reserve provided emergency support to prevent disorderly failure.
Documented company / regulator response: The New York Fed's official history explains the intervention and the underlying liquidity stress.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Stress-test collateral calls under extreme spread moves, cap wrong-way risk and maintain liquidity against collateral obligations rather than expected ultimate losses.
LinkedIn post angle: A contract can be profitable on paper and still bankrupt you before it matures.

Company profile: US energy trader and utility company whose collapse followed large-scale accounting fraud.
Documented business problem: The SEC charged senior leadership with schemes to falsify Enron's reported performance and financial condition.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Complex structures, conflicts of interest and a culture that rewarded earnings optics weakened transparency and challenge.
Business impact / signal: Enron filed for bankruptcy in 2001; SEC proceedings followed against senior executives.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC release records charges concerning falsified financial performance and condition.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Require transparent related-party disclosure, independent valuation of structured entities and board-level scrutiny of earnings-to-cash conversion.
LinkedIn post angle: When the organisation optimises the story told to investors, the operating reality can disappear.

Company profile: Indian private-sector bank that expanded its loan book before suffering rising stress and a capital shortfall.
Documented business problem: The RBI cited a steady decline in the bank's financial position, inability to raise capital for loan losses and governance concerns.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Aggressive loan growth is unsafe when underwriting quality, concentration limits and provisioning do not keep pace.
Business impact / signal: RBI imposed a moratorium and later announced a reconstruction scheme with SBI as the lead investor.
Documented company / regulator response: RBI's press releases document the moratorium and reconstruction plan.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Tie loan growth to vintage-level loss rates, independent credit approval and capital buffers; intervene before deposit confidence becomes the constraint.
LinkedIn post angle: The real cost of weak underwriting often appears long after the loan was booked.

Company profile: Indian housing-finance company that borrowed from markets and lenders to fund housing and other loans.
Documented business problem: The RBI superseded the board amid governance concerns and defaults on payment obligations.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): In a leveraged financial institution, weak governance and opaque asset quality can turn confidence into a liquidity problem.
Business impact / signal: RBI appointed an administrator and initiated insolvency proceedings under the applicable framework.
Documented company / regulator response: The RBI press release documents the board supersession and stated concerns.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Strengthen borrower-level audit trails, related-party controls, maturity matching and independent board risk oversight.
LinkedIn post angle: For a lender, governance is part of credit quality—not a separate compliance department.

Company profile: Indian IT-services company whose founder admitted that reported financial statements were falsified.
Documented business problem: The company disclosed serious irregularities in financial reporting, including overstated cash balances and receivables.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The board, auditor and internal control environment failed to challenge management representations and reconcile reported cash with independent evidence.
Business impact / signal: The government superseded the board and appointed a new board to stabilise the business and protect stakeholders.
Documented company / regulator response: SEBI and Government of India records document the investigation and board intervention.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Independently confirm bank balances, rotate sensitive control owners, strengthen audit committee access and protect whistleblowers.
LinkedIn post angle: A clean dashboard is worthless if the source data is not independently verified.

Company profile: Indian infrastructure and financial-services group with multiple subsidiaries and long-duration projects.
Documented business problem: Group entities defaulted on debt as delayed projects and reduced cash inflows weakened the ability to refinance obligations.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Long-gestation infrastructure assets were financed through borrowing that required continued refinancing; project delays weakened liquidity at the group level.
Business impact / signal: The government moved to replace the board and stabilise the group through a resolution process.
Documented company / regulator response: A parliamentary answer records defaults by group entities and the context.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Match project-level cash flows with debt maturities, maintain subsidiary-level liquidity visibility and stress-test refinancing availability.
LinkedIn post angle: A group can appear diversified while its subsidiaries are connected by the same refinancing risk.
Evidence type: Primary – Government of India parliamentary document

Company profile: Indian full-service airline launched in 2005 with premium service positioning and later a low-cost subsidiary strategy.
Documented business problem: Kingfisher accumulated heavy debt, struggled to meet operating payments and stopped flying in 2012.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A premium service cost base, high fixed commitments and a confusing shift toward a low-cost format weakened the economics; growth and image were not matched by financial discipline.
Business impact / signal: Its licence was suspended and the airline ceased operations; lenders pursued recovery.
Documented company / regulator response: CAG and academic case sources document the shutdown, unpaid dues and financial strain.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use route-level contribution economics, cash buffers for fuel and lease obligations, and prohibit expansion that depends on uncommitted refinancing.
LinkedIn post angle: A premium brand cannot survive on brand image when it cannot pay for fuel, aircraft and people.

Company profile: Indian full-service carrier that once held a leading position before low-cost competition expanded.
Documented business problem: Jet Airways lost share and profitability as low-cost carriers expanded; it was grounded in April 2019 amid debt and funding pressure.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The business struggled to align its full-service cost base, acquisitions, pricing and fleet choices with a market shifting toward lower fares.
Business impact / signal: Operations were suspended in April 2019 and insolvency proceedings followed.
Documented company / regulator response: Academic research and reporting document competition, acquisition burden, debt and the shutdown.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Rebuild around profitable route clusters and fleet commonality; avoid using acquisition scale to compensate for weak route contribution.
LinkedIn post angle: In a low-fare market, service differentiation must earn its cost premium route by route.

Company profile: Indian edtech group that expanded through acquisitions and large-scale customer acquisition before facing creditor and governance disputes.
Documented business problem: Public insolvency proceedings and disputes over dues, governance and financial reporting created uncertainty for creditors, employees and business partners.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Fast acquisition-led expansion increases the need for consolidated controls, transparent audited accounts, cash discipline and clear creditor communication.
Business impact / signal: The company faced insolvency-related legal proceedings; the cited IBBI order concerns a specific dispute and should not be treated as a complete account of every allegation.
Documented company / regulator response: The IBBI court record documents the specific BCCI-related settlement and insolvency appeal context.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Publish complete audited consolidated accounts, reconcile creditor claims, simplify the group structure and run a time-bound resolution plan.
LinkedIn post angle: A startup's growth story stops working when stakeholders cannot reconcile the numbers.

Company profile: Indian auto-service startup that built a network of garages and raised venture capital.
Documented business problem: The founders acknowledged financial irregularities in company statements; the company cut a large share of its workforce.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The case illustrates how aggressive growth narratives can outrun accounting discipline, financial controls and investor reporting.
Business impact / signal: The company announced layoffs and investors pursued a reset of governance and operations.
Documented company / regulator response: The Emerald case study describes the founder's admission and workforce reduction.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Introduce independent finance leadership, verified unit economics by workshop, monthly cash controls and investor-grade audit trails before scaling locations.
LinkedIn post angle: A marketplace can grow faster than its controls—and then discover that growth was hiding the problem.

Company profile: Indian hyperlocal delivery startup backed by investors including Reliance Retail.
Documented business problem: Dunzo faced severe cash constraints, cut staff and later its app and website went offline.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The company expanded its service promise and geography while carrying high delivery, marketing and technology costs; order growth did not guarantee contribution margin.
Business impact / signal: It reduced operations and workforce; the app and website went offline in January 2025.
Documented company / regulator response: Contemporary reporting describes the company's cash burn, funding and shutdown.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Prioritise dense neighbourhoods, charge for delivery complexity, raise basket size and enforce positive contribution margins before adding cities.
LinkedIn post angle: More orders do not save a delivery business if each order consumes more cash than it creates.

Company profile: Separate banking entity associated with the Paytm ecosystem; it held deposits and operated payment-bank services.
Documented business problem: RBI first imposed business restrictions in 2024 and cancelled the bank's licence in April 2026, citing serious supervisory and licensing concerns.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A regulated bank must maintain continuous compliance, depositor protection and governance independent of the wider consumer-app brand.
Business impact / signal: RBI cancelled the Payments Bank licence and later moved toward winding-up proceedings; this is not the same as saying the listed parent One97 Communications itself had its licence cancelled.
Documented company / regulator response: RBI's official release records the licence cancellation and stated grounds.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Separate regulated-entity governance, reconcile all customer balances, close compliance findings promptly and protect continuity of payments for users.
LinkedIn post angle: A consumer brand and a regulated bank are not the same thing. Their controls cannot be blended.

Company profile: Swedish battery manufacturer aiming to supply large-scale battery cells for the European EV industry.
Documented business problem: Northvolt filed for bankruptcy in Sweden after production ramp problems, funding pressure, supply-chain disruption and changing demand conditions.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The company faced a capital-intensive scale-up where factory yield, customer qualification and working capital had to improve simultaneously.
Business impact / signal: Northvolt filed for bankruptcy in March 2025.
Documented company / regulator response: The company's bankruptcy statement listed financing constraints, production ramp and market conditions among the factors.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Stage factory expansion by proven yield and customer acceptance; protect working capital and diversify critical suppliers and offtake commitments.
LinkedIn post angle: A gigafactory is not a business until it can repeatedly produce qualified cells at competitive cost.

Company profile: Chinese fintech group operating payments, lending and wealth-management services linked to Alipay.
Documented business problem: Ant Group's planned IPO was suspended after regulatory changes and scrutiny of the company's business model and risk controls.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A fintech that scales credit and financial services through a technology platform still carries banking-like systemic and capital risks.
Business impact / signal: The Shanghai Stock Exchange suspended the IPO in November 2020 and cited material regulatory developments.
Documented company / regulator response: The exchange's official notice documents the suspension.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Stress-test credit exposures, align capital and consumer-protection rules with the economic substance of products, and engage regulators before listing.
LinkedIn post angle: A technology platform may scale like software, but its financial risks scale like finance.

Company profile: Indian low-cost airline with a fleet and route network exposed to high fixed costs and intense fare competition.
Documented business problem: SpiceJet approached a liquidity crisis, had to reduce its fleet and struggled to fund fuel and operating expenses.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Low fares and overcapacity can reduce asset utilisation and cash generation; delayed external funding then turns a margin problem into a fleet problem.
Business impact / signal: The airline underwent a management and funding reset under Ajay Singh, with a plan to recover routes and fleet utilisation.
Documented company / regulator response: The ISB case describes the near-shutdown crisis and revival plan.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Build a route-by-route cash contribution model, preserve profitable routes, negotiate lessor terms and retain liquidity for fuel and maintenance.
LinkedIn post angle: For an airline, a parked aircraft is not just idle capacity. It is cash burn.
Evidence type: Academic case – Indian School of Business

Company profile: Indian low-cost airline that suspended operations in May 2023 and entered insolvency proceedings.
Documented business problem: Go First cited engine supply problems and operational constraints while facing debt and liquidity pressure; it ceased flying in May 2023.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A concentrated engine-supplier dependency can become existential when there is limited fleet substitution, spare-engine availability or liquidity runway.
Business impact / signal: The airline filed for insolvency and stopped operations; the precise responsibility for engine issues was disputed.
Documented company / regulator response: An AIMA research report summarises the case and the role of engine supply, debt and liquidity.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Stress-test supplier concentration, lease obligations and cash runway; maintain contingency fleet access and a recovery plan for prolonged parts shortages.
LinkedIn post angle: Supplier risk becomes business-survival risk when the business has no financial runway.

Company profile: Amazon launched a premium smartphone in 2014 with shopping and 3D-interface features.
Documented business problem: The Fire Phone failed to attract sustained demand; Amazon leadership later acknowledged that the launch price was wrong.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The product asked customers to pay a premium for features that were not compelling enough to overcome the strength of iOS and Android ecosystems.
Business impact / signal: Amazon discounted the device heavily and wrote down inventory.
Documented company / regulator response: Amazon's former devices executive publicly acknowledged the pricing mistake in post-launch commentary.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Test willingness to pay against real alternatives, launch with a sharp customer job-to-be-done and validate developer and app support before premium pricing.
LinkedIn post angle: A product is not differentiated just because its feature list is different.

Company profile: The Coca-Cola Company changed the formula of its flagship cola in 1985 after taste tests favoured the new formula.
Documented business problem: Consumers rejected the replacement formula despite positive blind taste-test results.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The research measured sip preference but missed the emotional and identity value of the original brand and the context of habitual consumption.
Business impact / signal: Coca-Cola restored the original formula as Coca-Cola Classic after 79 days.
Documented company / regulator response: The historical record documents the launch, backlash and reversal.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Combine blind taste tests with in-home use, brand attachment research and choice experiments that include the existing product as a reference.
LinkedIn post angle: Customer research can be technically correct and strategically incomplete.

Company profile: German sportswear group whose Yeezy collaboration generated significant sales and brand attention.
Documented business problem: After the partnership ended, Adidas was left with a large stock of Yeezy products and uncertainty about how to sell or write down inventory.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A concentrated product collaboration can create both demand upside and partner-reputation, inventory and concentration risk.
Business impact / signal: Adidas chose to sell portions of remaining inventory rather than write off all stock, donating proceeds to selected organisations.
Documented company / regulator response: Adidas' official results and annual report describe the inventory and sales decision.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Set partner concentration limits, maintain exit clauses and model unsold-inventory exposure before building capacity around a single collaboration.
LinkedIn post angle: A hit collaboration can become a supply-chain liability when the partnership ends overnight.
Evidence type: Primary – company press release / annual report

Company profile: Global sportswear company shifting between direct-to-consumer digital sales and wholesale retail partners.
Documented business problem: Nike disclosed inventory and channel-mix pressures and a need to rebalance digital, wholesale and full-price selling.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A DTC strategy can improve data and customer ownership, but pulling back from wholesale too quickly can reduce reach, discovery and product distribution.
Business impact / signal: Nike said it was reinvesting in wholesale and repositioning digital as a full-price platform while clearing excess inventory.
Documented company / regulator response: The FY2026 SEC filing describes channel strategy and inventory actions.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Segment products by channel role, measure full-price sell-through and protect wholesale relationships where they add reach and demand discovery.
LinkedIn post angle: Owning the customer is not the same as owning every transaction channel.

Company profile: US sportswear brand selling through wholesale partners and direct-to-consumer channels.
Documented business problem: Revenue declined across wholesale and DTC channels, and the company announced restructuring to improve financial and operational efficiency.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A brand can lose momentum when assortment, product differentiation and channel execution fail to create enough full-price demand.
Business impact / signal: Under Armour disclosed a restructuring plan and efficiency actions.
Documented company / regulator response: The FY2025 SEC filing provides revenue trends and restructuring context.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Narrow the product range around hero categories, improve inventory productivity and measure channel profitability after promotions.
LinkedIn post angle: When both wholesale and DTC soften, the problem may be the proposition—not just the channel.

Company profile: UK supermarket group operating a large grocery and general-merchandise business.
Documented business problem: Tesco overstated expected profits by about £250m through the acceleration of commercial income and delayed recognition of costs.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The issue exposed weak financial controls over supplier income, accounting cut-off and management pressure around short-term earnings.
Business impact / signal: Tesco restated expectations, investigated the issue and faced regulatory proceedings; the FRC later closed its investigation after enforcement action.
Documented company / regulator response: Tesco's trading update and FRC releases document the overstatement and investigation.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Reconcile supplier income to cash and contractual evidence, separate commercial negotiation from accounting approval and review cut-off independently.
LinkedIn post angle: Revenue quality is a process-control question, not just an accounting question.

Company profile: Global media group operating studios, parks, linear networks and Disney+ streaming.
Documented business problem: Direct-to-consumer streaming generated large operating losses before returning to operating profitability in FY2024.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Subscriber growth alone did not cover content, marketing, technology and distribution costs. The unit needed pricing, bundles, ad-supported tiers and more disciplined content economics.
Business impact / signal: Disney's DTC operating result moved from a loss of roughly $2.5bn in FY2023 to a profit in FY2024.
Documented company / regulator response: Disney's annual report and earnings release document the improvement.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Manage streaming on contribution margin and cohort lifetime value; allocate content by retention and engagement, not just launch-day buzz.
LinkedIn post angle: The streaming question is no longer only 'How many subscribers?' but 'What does each subscriber contribute?'
Evidence type: Primary – company annual report / earnings release

Company profile: Global audio-streaming platform that invested heavily in podcast studios, content and exclusive deals.
Documented business problem: After a period of heavy investment, Spotify reduced its podcast organisation and later announced a workforce reduction to improve cost discipline.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): The business needed to turn audience reach and podcast investment into durable monetisation rather than assume that content scale automatically created margin.
Business impact / signal: Spotify changed its podcast approach toward tailored partnerships and announced a 17% workforce reduction in December 2023.
Documented company / regulator response: Spotify's newsroom announcements document the organisational changes and rationale.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Invest in content with measurable incremental listening, ad yield and retention; use milestone-based contracts and sunset deals that do not meet return thresholds.
LinkedIn post angle: An audience strategy becomes a business strategy only when it creates repeatable revenue.

Company profile: Snap Inc. operates Snapchat, an advertising-supported social platform with a younger user base.
Documented business problem: Snap's filings show that advertising represented the great majority of revenue—about 87% in FY2025, compared with 91% in FY2024 and 96% in FY2023.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): This concentration leaves the platform exposed to advertiser cycles, measurement changes and competition for performance budgets; audience growth alone does not diversify the revenue base.
Business impact / signal: The SEC filing quantifies the reliance on advertising, making revenue diversification and advertiser outcomes central strategic issues.
Documented company / regulator response: Snap continued investing in performance advertising, measurement and subscription features; the filing provides the revenue mix but does not claim the diversification challenge is solved.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Build durable non-ad revenue where users show willingness to pay, improve advertiser ROI and stress-test the business against a sharp decline in ad budgets.
LinkedIn post angle: When nearly all revenue depends on advertising, user growth is not the same as revenue resilience.

Company profile: US online personal-styling retailer combining data science, human stylists and apparel fulfilment.
Documented business problem: Active clients and revenue declined as the company faced challenges in acquisition, retention and conversion.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Personalisation is only valuable when it reliably creates purchases and repeat behaviour; weak assortment, fit or perceived value can make an expensive acquisition funnel unprofitable.
Business impact / signal: Management identified retention, acquisition, conversion and client experience as operating priorities.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC filings quantify client and revenue trends and discuss retention and conversion challenges.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Measure repeat purchase by cohort, improve fit and recommendation feedback loops, and reduce acquisition spend on low-retention segments.
LinkedIn post angle: Personalisation is not the outcome. Repeat purchase is the outcome.

Company profile: Meta's Facebook platform relied on third-party applications and large-scale personal-data processing.
Documented business problem: The Cambridge Analytica episode and related disclosures exposed weaknesses in third-party data access, user consent and privacy governance.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): A platform's growth model can create incentives to expand data access faster than governance and user understanding evolve.
Business impact / signal: The FTC imposed a $5bn penalty and broad privacy requirements; the SEC also settled disclosure-related charges.
Documented company / regulator response: FTC and SEC releases document the penalties and findings.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use privacy-by-design, least-privilege access for apps, auditable consent and independent oversight of data-sharing partners.
LinkedIn post angle: Data access is a product feature until a governance failure turns it into a trust crisis.

Company profile: Global mobility and delivery platform connecting riders, drivers, couriers and merchants.
Documented business problem: Uber disclosed rising insurance-related costs and cost of revenue, creating pressure on marketplace economics.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): More trips can increase revenue and also increase claims exposure. The business needs pricing, driver safety and insurance reserving to improve together.
Business impact / signal: Uber disclosed higher insurance expense and operational initiatives in its annual filing.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC 10-K quantifies insurance-related cost increases and other cost-of-revenue drivers.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Use trip-level risk pricing, safety interventions, claims analytics and geographic contribution-margin reviews.
LinkedIn post angle: Growth is not profitable when every additional trip brings an unpriced risk obligation.

Company profile: US ride-hailing platform competing with Uber for riders and drivers.
Documented business problem: Lyft's insurance costs rose materially with ride volume and higher per-mile insurance rates.
Root-cause analysis (interpretation): Marketplace scale can magnify insurance costs if pricing and risk selection do not adjust quickly enough to the true loss experience.
Business impact / signal: Lyft reported increased insurance costs while revenue also grew; the filing links changes to higher rates and volume.
Documented company / regulator response: The SEC 10-K provides the insurance-cost movement and drivers.
Recommended management fix (not necessar: Price rides using current insurance cost by city and vehicle class; improve fraud and claims prevention and adjust incentives to reflect risk.
